Chapter 7: The Joy and Challenge of Deep Work
You know that feeling when you’re so absorbed in something, you lose all track of time? Hours just fly by, and it’s like the rest of the world disappears. That’s deep work—and honestly, it’s getting harder to find.
These days, distractions are everywhere. Notifications pop up, your phone buzzes, emails pile up, and it feels like you’re being pulled in every direction at once. It’s easy to end up just skimming the surface of your day, never really settling into anything meaningful. And when that happens, there’s often this restless, unsettled feeling—like nothing ever really gets finished.
But every now and then, someone manages to carve out a little oasis of focus. They might shut the door, silence their phone, and decide to pour all their attention into something they care about. Maybe it’s writing, tackling a tricky problem, or diving into a creative project. At first, it can feel uncomfortable—your brain wants to wander, to check for something easier or more exciting.
If you stick with it, though, something shifts. The background noise fades, and you settle into a deeper rhythm. Suddenly, you’re making real progress. The work itself becomes rewarding, and everything else just slips away. You feel present, alive, and deeply engaged. Most people don’t realize just how nourishing this experience can be—or how much they miss it when it’s gone.
Deep work isn’t only about getting more done. It’s about connecting—to what you’re doing, to yourself, and even to something bigger than you. It’s a way of respecting your own attention, choosing to go deep instead of spreading yourself thin. The satisfaction you get from this kind of focus is different than the quick buzz of checking off a to-do list. It sticks with you, quietly shaping how you see yourself and where you fit in the world.
Of course, making time for deep work means giving some things up. You’ve got to say “no” to those constant distractions and the quick hits of satisfaction that come from always being plugged in. It means accepting that some things just won’t get done right away, and that’s okay.
But here’s the thing: it’s worth it. Over time, people who protect that space for deep work find their days feel richer and more meaningful. Instead of always chasing after more, they find real joy in doing one thing well. The challenge is real—but so is the reward.
